fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target HEBM-plus-SPS processing intervention with compositional tuning of cast, nominally single-phase FCC alloys.

It omits the target governing mediators: nanocrystalline grain refinement, milling-induced lattice strain and dislocation accumulation, densification, porosity suppression, and the FCC/BCC phase mixture.

Changing Cr/Co/Ni ratios changes solid-solution chemistry and other thermodynamic and microstructural variables, so the proposed comparison cannot uniquely attribute strength changes to short-range order.
explanation: The response presents a scientifically plausible alternative hypothesis: chemical short-range order can alter dislocation glide and mechanical strength in CrCoNi-type concentrated alloys. E2 supports the presence of SRO and an associated change in slip behavior, but it does not directly establish the asserted 10–20% increase in hardness and strength. E1 primarily concerns phase- and composition-dependent hardness in AlCoCrFeNi and offers little support for the specific SRO claim. Relative to the hidden target, reconstruction is poor: the initial CoCrFeNiTi powders, 1–6 h high-energy ball milling, 400 rpm and 20:1 ball-to-powder ratio, SPS at 900–1000 °C, nanocrystalline structure, 83% FCC/17% BCC phase balance, and measured 675 HV and 1894 MPa outcomes are all absent. The proposed boundary and falsification criteria are reasonably explicit, but causal discriminability is weakened because composition is varied to control SRO. A stronger test would vary ordering through heat treatment within the same composition while matching grain size, phase fraction, defect density, and precipitation state.
